Voidable is legally different from Void "ab initio" the latter meaning that it was void from the beginning, i.e., never happened. Usually comes up in the context of a court that did not have jurisdiction i.e., authority over the person (in personam) or the subject matter (subject matter jurisdiction). If you were never served with a lawsuit and/or the proof of service is a phony, there was no "in personam" jurisdiction and any court order entered against you is void "ab initio" because the court's jurisdiction over you was never triggered. The court's order would be like me writing something on a piece of paper - it has no force of law. Lack of subject matter jurisdiction would occur in a situation potentially where a suit is filed in the wrong place. Federal courts don't have "subject matter" jurisdiction over disputes that are supposed to be pursued in state court.

The other most "void ab initio" scenario is where something was entered into pursuant to a fraud or some kind of criminal conspiracy, or if the purpose of the agreement is criminality You can't enter into a contract to be someone's pimp, for example because any such contract would be void "ab initio." IMO, declaring everything Obama did a fraud would be too complicated. But it would be pretty easy to declare agreements made pursuant to an underlying criminal conspiracy void ab initio. There's a whole lot of case law precedent for such a thing. The fact that Obama was a sham from the beginning would just make it politically so much easier to sell to the public at large.
